source.title: Bayesian Neural Scaling Law Extrapolation with Prior-Data Fitted Networks
source.authors: Dong-Woo Lee; Dongbok Lee; Steven Adriaensen; Juho Lee; Sung Ju Hwang; Frank Hutter; Seon Joo Kim; Haebeom Lee

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or document mismatch; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates extrapolation on existing scaling curves, including double-descent curves, and compares simple power-law fit families with more flexible forms. Its results qualify how reliably a single power-law form extrapolates; it does not reproduce parameter/token/compute scaling sweeps.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates held-out curve extrapolation on existing datasets, including image and language tasks, ColPret, nanoGPT-Bench, and double descent. This bears on extrapolation and curve shape. It does not itself run controlled language-model sweeps over parameter count, training tokens, or compute, or test compute-optimal allocations. The paper also reports results for many other estimators and metrics; the rows below focus on the reported M1, M4, and BNSL extrapolation results relevant to power-law fit and curve-shape claims.
record.test_reason: The study's comparisons of fitted functional forms and its analysis of non-monotonic empirical curves bear on V5 and the curve-shape component of V7. Its extrapolation benchmarks do not establish V2's prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger. Reporting a new extrapolator's performance alone would not test these claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors conclude that NSL-PFN generally improves extrapolation accuracy and uncertainty estimation, especially in data-limited and complex double-descent settings. Their main-text exceptions specifically name MCMC(M4) on NMT and point-estimation M4 on LM. These conclusions concern extrapolator performance, not proof of universal power laws or predictions across orders of magnitude.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates Bayesian and point-estimation curve extrapolators on existing datasets. It does not reproduce the original parameter/token/compute sweeps or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and curve shape affect performance. For BNSL, the authors also report sensitivity to validation split and cropping choices (Appendix C, Table 10); the main reported BNSL results use validation on the last 10% of context without cropping.

fits_no_version.finding: All extracted LL values are Bayesian MCMC results, measuring predictive accuracy together with uncertainty quality.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Predictive density and uncertainty quality vary among Bayesian scaling-curve extrapolators.

fits_no_version.finding: The benchmarks evaluate extrapolation along existing curves without documenting V2's required orders-of-magnitude gap between fitting and predicted runs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fitted curve families differ in their accuracy on held-out higher-resource portions of empirical scaling curves.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267
record.problems: The reported results are extrapolation errors averaged across existing curves, not controlled scaling sweeps over parameters, tokens, and compute. Several results are dataset aggregates, and no universal threshold for an adequate extrapolation error is specified. The authors note failed BNSL trials from overflow in some settings and uncertainty in BNSL implementation details.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 2-4 also report M2, M3, LC-PFN, MCMC variants, and the proposed NSL-PFN; these are omitted to stay focused on representative simple power-law, saturating-power-law, and broken-power-law fits. Additional BB results, table averages, active-learning results, cutoff plots, calibration, and prior ablations are not extracted. Appendix C Table 10 reports BNSL fit-choice variations (validation split and cropping); these are summarized in method_sensitivity rather than added as rows.

untested.parts: No reported analysis establishes held-out language-model loss scaling over several orders of magnitude while verifying that the other resources are not bottlenecks. Reusing existing curves does not itself preclude testing V1, but the required conditions are not demonstrated.

The paper evaluates held-out portions of empirical curves, but does not establish predictions of runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitting runs. Relative extrapolator performance cannot establish that scale-gap claim.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation or scaling exponents for that allocation are measured.
No fixed-parameter comparison isolating depth, width, or other architecture details.
No results establishing the power-law form for video, repeated-data training, or all fine-tuning and transfer regimes. The tested vision and translation settings cannot establish universality.
No direct analysis of downstream performance against pretraining loss or model scale. The downstream IC and BB curves vary training-data exposure instead.
No estimates of changes in scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits, and no direct reconciliation of Kaplan and Hoffmann. The evidence concerns functional-form adequacy and fitting sensitivity.

record.verdict_notes: No files or external sources were accessed. Every LL row was misassigned to its point-estimation counterpart; the tables report LL only for Bayesian methods. Table 10 fitting-choice results, BB results, and cutoff analyses are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing. ColPret excludes one excessively noisy curve and one saturating curve, limiting representativeness. Dataset-average RMSLE has no stated universal success threshold; nonzero error alone does not establish partial, absent, or reversed scaling.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not conduct controlled sweeps of held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, training tokens, or compute while holding the other factors non-bottlenecked.
It evaluates extrapolation on existing curves, not a controlled test of runs orders of magnitude larger than fitting runs across parameter-count, token-count, and compute scales.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is tested.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count is reported.
The study evaluates existing image, language, and other curve datasets, but does not test video, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer as training regimes for the same power law.
It does not test downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss or model scale; some included downstream-task curves vary with training-data size.
The study reports extrapolation differences among fit families and fitting choices, and tests curves with bends, but does not estimate the original studies' exponents or compute-optimal splits.
